Usenet to Voat, Eternal Exodus of Internet Communities

*I feel it should be noted that these articles attempt to be as factual as possible, but some things are slightly simplified or omitted for the sake of brevity.

I do not delve into the legal repercussions and responsibilities for the hosting services of content. I don't feel I have enough knowledge in the legal nuances and wish to avoid a regional bias. Some countries hold servers to account severely by saying that content posted on a website turns the site into a 'publisher' that is responsible for making sure all their users to obey the law.

Many of the events I describe are presented as blocks of time with concrete start and stop points. The truth of the matter is more complicated, with many technologies and websites overlapping in their time frames, and transitional processes sometimes taking years of time. However, if one was to focus on the time frames extensively, I feel it would detract from the bigger picture I am trying to paint with these words.

Knowingly, I gloss over social networking as it will be included in a future article.

I don't bring up the dilution of quality in a community because of the size of the community. Obviously, this is a glaring issue that plays a major role in the movement of people through online communities. However, I believe that this is more a subjective problem than an actual one. Modern content sites allow you to filter yourself down to specific subtopics (and thus, smaller communities that can control their content amongst themselves). By that rationale, a user is responsible for taking charge of their own experience and anything they are exposed to is voluntary.

And, most obviously, this is just one view of the story that is larger than any single person could hope to document.*

If you met me in real life and asked me to define my heritage, I would probably tell you that I'm of Irish-Finnish descent and consider myself Canadian to the core. I might mention my lack of religious upbringing. Maybe I'll talk about my origins in British Columbia. But those are only half-truths.

To be honest, I consider my heritage to have nothing to do with race, nationality, or religion. I am a proud citizen of the Internet.

As long as I can remember, I've had a computer connected to the Internet. I'm not quite as old as the true 'old dogs' that were involved in the initial rise of the Web, but my first memory of the Internet involved a 286 hooked up to a 9600 baud modem (Oh the glory later in life when we moved up to 28.8k!). I discovered Usenet as a playground to explore filled with knowledgeable people in diverse areas.

Content makes the Web go round. It's what has always been, and continues to be, the most exciting prospect of the internet. Strangers, sometimes thousands of miles apart, sharing their stories and connecting to each other. The people you met existed only as the words they typed, solely on the merit of the strings of characters they put together. It was hard for to understand racism, sexism, and prejudice when a person only existed upon their chosen actions they presented on the net.

In the beginning, if you wanted to know how something worked or how to do something you would make a post to alt.sometopic on Usenet and hopefully someone would reply. Eventually, a lot of the common questions were answered and all you had to do was dig through the vast swaths of information in order to find your answer. But it wasn't all dry and technical. People posted links to funny, or sometimes disturbing pictures. As the World Wide Web grew so did the number of links to external websites with articles, opinions, and news. Jokes were told. You could find more entertainment than you could ever consume all in a single place. This was our content.

Does all this sound familiar?

There were warning signs the end of Usenet was coming but it seemed like the change happened overnight. Mixed amongst the conversations were poorly written posts of a line or two, with a link that was obviously a poor advertisement. Those types of posts, the garbage ones, became exponentially more frequent, quickly, obviously being submitted by scripts instead of humans. Some were advertisements for products. Some were phishers looking for a victim. Some were straight-up links to malware. But eventually the bots and scripts outnumbered the men and women of Usenet. Given that the NNTP protocol was very basic, it became very difficult to sort out the positive information from the wasted bytes. Eventually, it wasn't worth the hassle and users moved on.

Usenet was dying. Sometime in the early to mid-nineties somebody got the idea that users would like to have a personal chunk of the Web carved out for themselves. Free personal web hosting services like Geocities and Tripod grew a massive user base. Everyone was teaching themselves HTML and creating links to each others' content. With nothing but an email address and armed with a little knowledge you could create a site about anything. Eventually, Making your own website became more of a niche thing as the Internet population increased. The flood of less technically-minded users meant that the majority of people were merely observing content as opposed to creating it. Who would want to waste their time learning to program a website?

(I'll admit, the first website I ever programmed for myself was a Sailor Moon fan website, complete with links to fan-fiction. Yes, I know. No, really, you don't have to tell me, I know.)

Up until this point, no one really had any idea of how to make money on the Web except the telephone companies charging for bandwidth. Internet access was becoming widely available as the costs for modems and connection plans plummeted to a level that was affordable to average consumers. Everyone knew there had to be a way to turn this technology into money, but there was uncertainty of how to do it. The financial aspect is now much more relevant – the costs are mounting and so far only a few businesses have successfully managed to create revenue from the Web.

(Minor Aside: Eventually, a vast majority of internet start-ups that had large amounts of capital invested into them on spec would fold after producing no revenue causing the dot-com bubble to burst.)

You can debate forever on who started social networking, but let's just say 'Friendster' and leave it at that; however, I would argue that the first network to be massively successful at attracting a substantial user base was MySpace.

MySpace allowed the average user to have a somewhat personal website where they could post pictures, audio and video, and link to anywhere else on the net. It simplified the process of having your own website by constraining your content to a set system of simplified rules, and self-perpetuated by allowing users to link to each other seamlessly and easily within their network. This allowed the people that were intimidated by the prospect of learning how to code HTML to have some of the benefits of their own website without having to read through technical manuals and tutorials.

But hardly anybody uses MySpace anymore (in comparison to their peak). What happened?

In 2005, News Corporation purchased MySpace and the monetization began. Though the site continued to grow for a couple years (peaking about 2007-2008), the user generated content it offered began to be overshadowed by the agenda to make it a giant digital movie and music flyer. Advertisements were becoming more intrusive on the site and censorship policies were being adopted. MySpace soon seemed to become nothing more than a network for companies to 'Shout Out' about their products and users began to flee in droves. Those wanting a more social networking experience moved to Facebook. But a large portion moved to the newer, anonymous, content aggregation ideas.

I'll give honourable mention to Fark here, but the real blockbuster of the content aggregation world was Digg. Content was suddenly flowing freely, moderated by a robust community, and the world seemed at peace. Digg grew to have a massive amount of users that were fervently loyal. But as with MySpace it too began to collapse under external pressures driven by attempts to generate revenue. The owners and admins, while pretending to involve the community in the process, began to make decisions contrary to the values and opinions of their user group. And then there was the overbearing plan to monetize the community by allowing 'partners' of Digg to inject advertisements into the content streams – an aggresive tactic to hawk products in the most blatant way possible. The great Digg migration begun.

Reddit picked up the bulk of Digg's users, calling itself a 'bastion of free speech.' The content community flourished in its new home, and after a short period of adjustment all was well.

Until the last couple of months.

It is no surprise to me that Reddit we see the same historical patterns that plagued MySpace and Digg as they began to monetize their servers. There are plenty of articles happening what's going on with Reddit, but the majority of them are highly politicized. In brief, a portion of the community (and especially the mods) were fed up with the presumptuous decision-making and hollow promises from the upper echelons that would not listen to their concerns. The removal of controversial subreddits, and most recently Yishan Wong's posting, have been signaling the advent of censorship on the site.

If you look at the history of MySpace and Digg, you'll see that Reddit already contain two out of three elements that drove their communities into spectres of what they were at their height. All that's left is for Reddit to sell off premium advertising space in an intrusive manner that detracts from the experience of the site as a whole.

It's not surprising then that users are instinctively flowing in droves over to Voat. In fact, it's right on time: if you look at the life cycles of all these websites you'll see that after about 3 years they hit a peak, begin to change, and then decline steadily for 3 years. Around 2018 I would expect Voat to be looking at the same thing.

So what's the problem then? Why can't we just create a stable online community with a business model that works? The problem is server and bandwidth costs. These web sites usually begin out with starry-eyed 20-somethings who have no money and dream of uniting people without barriers. They idolize the old values of the original Internet pioneers. Ideals are wonderful, but ambitious beliefs in humanity don't keep the lights on, unfortunately. The prohibitive cost of running a large centralized site will eventually put it out of reach of most people without additional financial support. Enter the advertisers with suitcases of money, and cue the admins of the site no longer listening to their community as they try to broker deals.

Though the benefit of advertising online is unknown, there are companies out there willing to pay to have their products shown – with caveats. The first and foremost is usually that the advertisement be in a way that 'forces' the end user to receive the message. A good example of this is advertisements on Youtube that are unable to be skipped. The audience is held captive waiting for their content and must give however much time the advertiser has bought for that block. On content web sites advertising usually becomes blended into the content stream, more often than not requiring preferential loading to the hosted content. The second issue that arises from advertisers is censorship. Advertisers are reluctant to back anything that could compromise their brand and have it associated with something offensive. They protect their product by ensuring that the environment that they buy space from is completely sanitized of anything that is outside of mainstream popular opinions. When a website brings in an advertiser they begin to lose control of their site and have to bend to the stipulations of their revenue agreements. There's no choice – the website needs the money and the advertisers, like predators, know it.

So what conclusions can we draw from all this? It seems that business and freedom of speech are incompatible on the internet. A content aggregation site, especially one that allows its users the freedom to post anything they want, will always be doomed to begin failing once the magnitude of the site reaches a point where monetization – advertisers – are necessary to come on board to cover the costs of their servers and bandwidth. Unless a new business model for centralized content aggregation emerges, we will be doomed to continue with user migrations across platforms as digital nomads. The worst part about it is that it ends like an episode from the first season of Battlestar Galactica – once the people have moved on, the advertising Cylons will inevitably follow.

I don't have the answers. I can't come up with a graceful solution. Is the answer to intensively specialize communities to limit the sizes and costs to something individuals can manage? Or maybe there's a way to force advertising to compromise and restrain it from destroying the spirit of a website. Maybe there's a billionaire altruist who wants to set up a trust fund. Hopefully someone smarter than I am who is reading this article will see this as a challenge and come up with something that will work in the future. It is paramount that we preserve freedom of speech on the internet. Without that, we will be completely lost.

Without our voices, we will lose our heritage.

This is the first of a series of articles in a series that I am writing. The following article is not intended for the passing consumer of the internet. It is intended for the generation that spends their time truly connecting with their fellow man in online communities. It is meant to be a voice observing what is happening in our interconnected digital world.
